extracted.intended_audience: poets, playwrights, and students of dramatic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing tragedy: construction of plot, recognition/reversal devices, diction, and stylistic choices to produce dramatic effect on stage. Emphasises unity, relevance of episodes, modes of recognition, and clarity of language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition should arise from natural incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Such is that in the Oedipus of Sophocles, and in the Iphigenia; these recognitions alone dispense with the artificial aid of tokens or amulets.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer recognitions that 'arise from the incidents ere the startling discovery is natural means.' Avoid artificial tokens or amulets as a means of recognition; example praise: Oedipus and Iphigenia. Natural recognitions are superior to contrived devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid false inference as the basis for recognition
rubrics_metrics.description: A composite kind of recognition or false inference… the expectation that A would recognise the bow is false inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on a character's incorrect inference (expectation that another will recognise something they have not seen) to manufacture recognition; such devices are less convincing than recognitions grounded in the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place the scene vividly before the poet's eyes
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should place the scene, as far as possible, before his eyes. In this way, seeing everything with the utmost vividness… he will be most unlikely to overlook inconsistencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visualize the stage action as a spectator to catch inconsistencies and ensure that incidents and stage business cohere; failing to 'see' the situation leads to stage errors (example: Carcinus — Amphiaraus on his way from the temple overlooked and offended the audience).

rubrics_metrics.name: Work out appropriate gestures and delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Again, the poet should work out his play, to the best of his power, with appropriate gestures; for those who feel emotion are most convincing through natural sympathy with the characters they represent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan gestures and delivery so actors' natural sympathy and agitation (anger, grief) produce lifelike reality; delivery/diction and physical acting are integral to poetic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sketch a general plan first, then fill in episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: He should first sketch its general outline, and then fill in the episodes and amplify in detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with a clear overall plot skeleton (general plan) before adding episodes; example: Iphigenia—overall structure governs how episodes should be introduced and resolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Episodes must be relevant to the action
rubrics_metrics.description: We must see that they are relevant to the action. In the drama, the episodes are short, but it is these that give extension to Epic poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include only episodes that advance or relate to the main action; avoid extraneous material or long digressions (episodic material is appropriate to epic, not drama).

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep episodes short and integrated in drama
rubrics_metrics.description: In the drama, the episodes are short… This is the essence of the plot; the rest is episode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatic episodes should be concise; long-form narrative expansion (an 'Epic structure' with multiplicity of plots) undermines stage effectiveness and often leads to failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain unity of plot — avoid epic multiplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Again, the poet should remember… and not make a Tragedy into an Epic structure. By an Epic structure I mean one with a multiplicity of plots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select a portion of a larger story rather than dramatising an entire epic; plays that attempt the whole tale (e.g., Fall of Troy) tend to fail. Unity of Complication and Unravelling defines identity of a tragedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish Complication and Unravelling
rubrics_metrics.description: By the Complication I mean all that extends from the beginning of the action and the part which marks the turning-point to good or bad fortune. The Unravelling is that which extends from the beginning of the change to the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure the plot so the Complication sets up the turning-point and the Unravelling carries the consequences to resolution. Use these parts to test plot identity and coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Reversal and Recognition skillfully (Complex tragedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four kinds of Tragedy, the Complex,… depending entirely on Reversal and Recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a 'complex' tragedy, base the action on well-crafted reversals of intention and recognitions; these devices generate powerful tragic effects when plausible and organically embedded in the plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of tragic motive: Pathetic and Ethical
rubrics_metrics.description: Pathetic (where the motive is passion)… Ethical (where the motives are ethical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the dominant motive of a play—passion-driven (pathetic) or moral/ethical—and shape incidents, speech, and character actions to serve that motive; examples: Ajax (pathetic), Phthiotides (ethical).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple tragedy: exclude purely spectacular element
rubrics_metrics.description: The fourth kind is the Simple <we here exclude the purely spectacular element>, exemplified by the Phorcides, the Prometheus, and scenes laid in Hades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'simple' tragedy relies on measured, non-spectacular means—focus on essential action rather than showy spectacle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine as many poetic merits as possible
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should endeavour, if possible, to combine all poetic merits; or failing that, the greatest number and those the most important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to include multiple virtues (plot, thought, diction, spectacle, song, character) and prioritize the most important when full combination is impossible; contemporary critics expect wide-ranging excellence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reversals should satisfy the moral sense and be probable
rubrics_metrics.description: This effect is produced when the clever rogue… is outwitted, or the brave villain defeated. Such an event is probable in Agathon’s sense of the word: 'it is probable that many things should happen contrary to… probability.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft reversals that feel morally satisfying and remain within the bounds of probability (even when surprising) to satisfy audience expectations and taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chorus must be integral to the action
rubrics_metrics.description: The chorus… should be an integral part of the whole, and may share in the action, in the manner not of Euripides but of Sophocles. Later poets' choral songs pertain as little to the subject as to that of any other tragedy; they are… mere interludes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the chorus to participate in and advance the drama; avoid choral interludes that are unrelated spectacle or interchangeable fragments from other plays.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thought: produce effects by speech (proof, refutation, feeling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Thought is included every effect which has to be produced by speech, the subdivisions being—proof and refutation; the excitation of the feelings, such as pity, fear, anger; the suggestion of importance or its opposite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design speeches to accomplish intellectual and emotional effects (argue, persuade, incite pity/fear); coordinate thought with rhetorical aims drawn from the Rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incidents should 'speak for themselves' without verbal exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: The dramatic incidents must be treated from the same points of view as the dramatic speeches… The only difference is, that the incidents should speak for themselves without verbal exposition; while the effects aimed at in speech should be produced by the speaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let actions on stage demonstrate plot facts and emotional stakes rather than relying on characters' expository speeches to tell what happened.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction must consider Modes of Expression but belongs to Delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: One branch of the inquiry treats of the Modes of Expression. But this province of knowledge belongs to the art of Delivery… It includes—for instance—what is a command, a prayer, a narrative, a threat, a question, an answer, and so forth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize different speech types and shape diction accordingly, coordinating with actors' delivery; the poet need not be faulted for confusions that properly belong to the art of delivery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perfection of style: clear without being mean
rubrics_metrics.description: The perfection of style is to be clear without being mean. The clearest style is that which uses only current or proper words; at the same time it is mean—witness the poetry of Cleophon and of Sthenelus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for clarity through current/proper words but avoid a mean or paltry diction; clarity should be dignified and appropriate to the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer current (proper) words; be cautious with strange or novelty words
rubrics_metrics.description: Every word is either current, or strange, or metaphorical, or ornamental, or newly-coined, or lengthened, or contracted, or altered. By a current or proper word I mean one which is in general use among a people; by a strange word, one which is in use in another country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use words familiar to the audience for clarity; metaphors and novel coinages can be used but with care and justified by poetic effect (examples and types of metaphor explained).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use metaphor by transference and analogy judiciously
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphor is the application of an alien name by transference either from genus to species, or from species to genus, or from species to species, or by analogy… Analogy or proportion is when the second term is to the first as the fourth to the third.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ metaphor through genus-species transference or proportion/analogy; metaphors may be qualified by adding the related term, and are legitimate even when no existing word fits the proportional term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word-formation: ornamental, newly-coined, lengthened, contracted, altered words
rubrics_metrics.description: A newly-coined word is one which has never been even in local use, but is adopted by the poet himself… A word is lengthened when its own vowel is exchanged for a longer one, or when a syllable is inserted. A word is contracted when some part of it is removed. An altered word is one in which part of the ordinary form is left unchanged, and part is re-cast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of different processes of coinage and alteration; such transformations are available to the poet but must serve clarity, diction, and poetic effect rather than novelty alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language units and their dramatic effect (letters to sentences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Language in general includes the following parts—Letter, Syllable, Connecting word, Noun, Verb, Inflexion or Case, Sentence or Phrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand how lowest-level language choices (letters, syllables, connecting words) feed into meter, diction, and the appropriateness of speech types; some of these inquiries properly belong to metre and delivery, but affect poetic style.
